images.filename: Din Lligwy and Plas Lligwy - two estate centres - geograph.org.uk - 755246.jpg
images.caption:
Din Lligwy and Plas Lligwy - two estate centres Din Lligwy has been described by the leading archaeologist Frances Lynch as being "a well-regulated 'estate centre' with houses and working buildings arranged within an imposing wall". It was the HQ of a local chieftain during the time of the Roman occupation and in many ways resembled a Roman villa. Later in the early medieval period the local chieftains made their home on what is now the site of Plas Lligwy.
    This photo has been taken along the eastern wall of Din Lligwy. The building in the foreground was a large barn which also doubled as a gateway to the villa.

images.filename: A round house at Din Lligwy - geograph.org.uk - 954037.jpg
images.caption: A round house at Din Lligwy This building is believed to be the main residential building of the Romano-British settlement of Din Lligwy.  This photo is almost identical to 218, however, I have submitted it because since that photo was taken in 2005 a large boulder has appeared behind the round house in my photo.  It may have fallen out of the perimeter wall to the left, but it would not be easy to move it by hand.

images.filename: Footpath to Din Lligwy-Din Llugwy - geograph.org.uk - 950801.jpg
images.caption: Footpath to Din Lligwy/Din Llugwy A small layby, at the side of this minor road west of Moelfre, allows parking for access to the Romano-British settlement known as Din Lligwy/Din Llugwy.  The footpath follows the field along the wall.  There are stone steps on the other side of the kissing gate, with more steps further on, so the route is not easy for the less able.  The shell of the medieval chapel of ease, Old Lligwy Chapel/Hen Capel Llugwy, is out of sight to the right.  The usual notices are in English and Welsh, which doubles the visual impact.

images.filename: Lane near Din Lligwy-Din Llugwy - geograph.org.uk - 951295.jpg
images.caption: Lane near Din Lligwy/Din Llugwy The lay-by allowing access to Din Lligwy/Din Llugwy and Old Lligwy Chapel/Hen Capel Llugwy is just out of sight on the left.  The medieval chapel of ease Old Lligwy Chapel/Hen Capel Llugwy can be seen through the gateway in the hedge. The sign for 'Caneuon y Cerrig/Songs from Stones' is a reference to an animated film created by artist Sean Harris in conjunction with visitors to Beaumaris Castle during August.  A trail associated with the project visits five sites, Din Lligwy/Din Llugwy being the fifth and therefore letter 'E'.
